concept.name: ACID Transaction Fundamentals

relationships.description: Connects ACID Transaction Fundamentals to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: ACID guarantees that database transactions execute as all-or-nothing units (Atomicity), preserve schema and domain invariants (Consistency), shield concurrent readers/writers from partial state (Isolation), and survive power loss once acknowledged (Durability) via write-ahead logging (WAL), `fsync`, and concurrency control (MVCC/2PL).
spark.keyTakeaway: ACID is not a binary switch: durability relies on WAL `fsync` before commit acknowledgment, while isolation is a tunable spectrum from `READ COMMITTED` to `SERIALIZABLE` trading lock/abort overhead for anomaly prevention.

concept.whyItMatters: Without ACID guarantees, concurrent requests and sudden process crashes corrupt financial ledgers, oversell finite inventory, and leave foreign-key relationships half-written. Understanding how engines implement ACID via MVCC, undo/redo logs, and lock managers lets you pick the lowest isolation level that still protects your invariants without choking throughput.
whenToUse: Double-entry financial ledgers, wallet transfers, and billing settlements where a debit without its matching credit is catastrophic.
Finite inventory, seat booking, and quota enforcement where concurrent requests race to claim the last available unit.
Multi-table state transitions (e.g., inserting an `orders` row, updating `inventory`, and appending an `outbox` event) that must succeed or roll back together.
whenNotToUse: High-volume clickstream, telemetry, or IoT sensor ingestion where losing or reordering a few milliseconds of unacknowledged events is acceptable for 10x write throughput.
Append-only event logs or analytics warehouses (ClickHouse, BigQuery) optimized for columnar batch scans rather than single-row transactional updates.
Globally distributed, sub-10ms-latency reads/writes where cross-region consensus (Paxos/Raft) and Two-Phase Commit (2PC) round-trips violate latency SLAs.
keyPoints: Atomicity is enforced via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) in PostgreSQL (`pg_wal`) or undo/redo logs in MySQL InnoDB: uncommitted changes are rolled back or ignored on crash recovery.

Consistency in ACID means the database moves from one valid state to another (enforcing `CHECK`, `UNIQUE`, and `FOREIGN KEY` constraints), though application-level invariants still require proper transaction boundaries.

Isolation prevents concurrency anomalies—dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, lost updates, phantom reads, and write skew—using either Two-Phase Locking (2PL) or Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC).

Durability requires flushing WAL buffers to non-volatile storage via `fsync()` (or `fdatasync()`) before returning `COMMIT OK` to the client; group commit amortizes this disk I/O across concurrent transactions.

Snapshot Isolation (`REPEATABLE READ` in PostgreSQL) eliminates dirty and non-repeatable reads without read locks, but still permits write skew unless upgraded to `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI) or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

examples.title: Double-Entry Wallet Transfer in PostgreSQL
examples.scenario: A payment service moves $250 from Account A (`balance = $400`) to Account B (`balance = $100`) while another request simultaneously tries to withdraw $300 from Account A.
examples.outcome: Wrapping both `UPDATE` statements in `BEGIN ... COMMIT` with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (ordered by `account_id` to prevent deadlocks) serializes access to Account A's row; the second transaction sees `$150`, fails the `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint, and rolls back cleanly.

examples.title: Flash-Sale Inventory Reservation Under Load
examples.scenario: 500 concurrent checkout workers attempt to decrement `stock_qty` on SKU-42 when only 3 units remain.
examples.outcome: Using an atomic `UPDATE inventory SET stock_qty = stock_qty - 1 WHERE sku = 'SKU-42' AND stock_qty > 0 RETURNING stock_qty` inside a transaction ensures exactly 3 workers succeed and 497 receive 0 rows affected, avoiding the classic read-then-write lost update.

tradeOffs.pro: `SERIALIZABLE` (via SSI in PostgreSQL) eliminates all anomalies including write skew without manual locking.
tradeOffs.con: Increases serialization failure (`SQLSTATE 40001`) abort rates under high contention, requiring client-side retry loops.

tradeOffs.pro: Synchronous WAL flush (`synchronous_commit = on`) guarantees zero committed data loss on power failure.
tradeOffs.con: Caps single-thread commit rate to disk IOPS/latency unless batched by group commit or NVMe write-back caches with BBU.

tradeOffs.factor: Single-Node ACID vs. Distributed Transactions (2PC / Spanner)
tradeOffs.pro: Single-node transactions execute in microseconds using local memory locks and a single WAL stream.
tradeOffs.con: Scaling writes past one primary requires 2PC or Raft/TrueTime coordination, adding network RTTs and coordinator-failure complexity.

failureModes.name: Write Skew Under Snapshot Isolation
failureModes.description: Two transactions read overlapping rows (e.g., two on-call doctors checking that at least 2 doctors remain on shift) and update disjoint rows (`doctor_1` and `doctor_2`), leaving 0 doctors on call.
failureModes.mitigation: Use `SERIALIZABLE` isolation (SSI detects rw-antidependency cycles) or lock a shared parent row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

failureModes.name: Lost Update in Read-Modify-Write
failureModes.description: Under `READ COMMITTED`, two threads read `balance = 100`, compute `100 + 20` and `100 - 30` in app memory, and both write back, silently overwriting the first update.
failureModes.mitigation: Perform arithmetic in SQL (`SET balance = balance + 20`), use `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, or use `REPEATABLE READ` (which aborts the second writer with a serialization error).

failureModes.name: Torn Pages on Power Loss
failureModes.description: A 16 KB InnoDB page or 8 KB Postgres page is only half-written to disk during a crash, corrupting B-tree pointers.
failureModes.mitigation: Enable `full_page_writes = on` (PostgreSQL) or the InnoDB doublewrite buffer so recovery can reconstruct any partially written page from a clean full-page image.

failureModes.name: MVCC Bloat & Transaction ID Wraparound
failureModes.description: An idle-in-transaction session holds an old snapshot open for hours, preventing `VACUUM` from reclaiming dead tuples and causing table bloat and latency cliffs.
failureModes.mitigation: Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (e.g., `30s`), `statement_timeout`, and monitor oldest `xmin` age and `autovacuum` lag.

commonMistakes: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` in PostgreSQL is free of anomalies—it is Snapshot Isolation, which still allows write skew.
Leaving transactions open across external HTTP/gRPC calls, holding row locks and MVCC snapshots for seconds instead of milliseconds.
Ignoring `SQLSTATE 40001` (serialization failure) and `40P01` (deadlock detected) instead of implementing bounded exponential-backoff retries.
Locking multiple rows in inconsistent orders across code paths, triggering avoidable deadlocks.
Disabling `fsync` or `synchronous_commit` in production benchmarks and forgetting to re-enable them before launch.

sections.content:
## The idea

Relational databases sit atop volatile RAM (buffer pools) and block-oriented disks that can fail mid-write while hundreds of clients mutate overlapping rows concurrently. **ACID**—Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability—is the contract that lets application engineers reason about multi-step state changes as if each transaction ran alone on an uncrashable machine.

In practice, engines implement ACID with two cooperating subsystems: **logging/recovery** (Write-Ahead Logging plus `fsync` for Atomicity and Durability) and **concurrency control** (2PL or MVCC + SSI for Isolation). Consistency is shared: the engine enforces declarative constraints (`UNIQUE`, `CHECK`, `FOREIGN KEY`), while the developer defines the transaction boundaries that preserve business invariants.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider transferring `$500` from `acct_101` (`$1,200`) to `acct_202` (`$300`) in PostgreSQL under `SERIALIZABLE`:

1. **Begin & Snapshot (`txid = 8421`)**: The transaction manager assigns `txid = 8421` and captures a snapshot (`xmin/xmax` visibility boundary). No data pages are modified yet.
2. **Row Locks & MVCC Versioning**: `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 500 WHERE id = 101` acquires an exclusive row lock on `acct_101`, marks the old tuple's `xmax = 8421`, and inserts a new tuple version (`balance = 700`, `xmin = 8421`) in the shared buffer pool. The same happens for `acct_202` (`balance = 800`).
3. **WAL Append**: Before any dirty heap page is flushed to disk, PostgreSQL appends redo/undo records (LSN `0/1A4F820` -> `0/1A4F910`) to the WAL buffer.
4. **Commit & `fsync`**: On `COMMIT`, the engine writes a `COMMIT 8421` record to `pg_wal` and issues `fsync()` (batched via group commit). Only after the NVMe controller acknowledges durability does the server send `COMMIT OK` to the client and release row locks.
5. **Crash or Rollback**: If power fails at step 3, `txid = 8421` has no `COMMIT` WAL record; on restart, its `xmin = 8421` tuples are invisible to all future snapshots and cleaned up by `VACUUM`.

edges.label: Append WAL Record

edges.description: Redo/full-page records are appended to WAL buffers ahead of any dirty data page flush.

edges.label: COMMIT
edges.title: Request Commit
edges.description: Client sends COMMIT after verifying all SQL statements and constraints succeeded.

edges.label: fsync(COMMIT)
edges.title: Flush WAL to Disk
edges.description: Group commit flushes the COMMIT record via fsync() to durable storage before acknowledging.

edges.title: Background Page Flush
edges.description: Checkpointer asynchronously flushes dirty buffer pages to heap files and advances the redo LSN.

data.caption: Write-Ahead Logging decouples fast in-memory MVCC page mutations from sequential `fsync()` durability on commit.

sections.content:
## Isolation levels & MVCC mechanics

ANSI SQL defines four isolation levels, though real engines implement them differently. Under **Two-Phase Locking (2PL)**, readers acquire shared (`S`) locks and writers acquire exclusive (`X`) locks, blocking each other. Under **MVCC** (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle), writers create new row versions instead of overwriting in place, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

- **`READ COMMITTED`** (Postgres/Oracle default): Each statement sees a fresh snapshot of committed data as of statement start. Prevents dirty reads, but allows non-repeatable reads and lost updates in read-modify-write patterns.
- **`REPEATABLE READ`** (MySQL InnoDB default; Snapshot Isolation in Postgres): The transaction holds one snapshot for its entire duration. Prevents non-repeatable reads and (in Postgres) phantom reads, but still allows **write skew** across disjoint rows.
- **`SERIALIZABLE`**: Guarantees an execution equivalent to some serial order. PostgreSQL uses **Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)**, tracking `SIREAD` predicate locks to abort transactions that form dangerous `rw`-antidependency cycles, avoiding 2PL's heavy read blocking.

## Isolation anomalies & engine behavior

| Isolation Level | Dirty Read | Non-Repeatable Read | Phantom Read | Write Skew | Typical Mechanism |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `READ UNCOMMITTED` | Possible | Possible | Possible | Possible | No read locks (rarely used) |
| `READ COMMITTED` | Prevented | Possible | Possible | Possible | Per-statement snapshot (PG) / short S-locks |
| `REPEATABLE READ` | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented in PG (InnoDB uses gap locks) | Possible in PG | Transaction-wide MVCC snapshot |
| `SERIALIZABLE` | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | Prevented | SSI (`SIREAD` locks in PG) or Strict 2PL + Gap Locks |

## Failure modes

1. **Deadlocks (`40P01`)**: Transaction T1 locks `acct_101` then requests `acct_202`; T2 locks `acct_202` then requests `acct_101`. The lock manager's wait-for graph detector kills one victim. *Fix*: Always lock entities in a canonical sort order (e.g., ascending `account_id`).
2. **Serialization Failures (`40001`)**: Under `REPEATABLE READ` or `SERIALIZABLE`, concurrent writers touching the same or conflicting predicate ranges trigger an abort. *Fix*: Wrap transactional entrypoints in an idempotent retry loop (3–5 attempts with jittered backoff).
3. **Long-Transaction MVCC Bloat**: A forgotten `BEGIN` idle in an interactive session or a 2-hour analytics query pins the global `xmin`, stalling `VACUUM` and inflating table sizes 5–10x.
4. **Cross-System Dual-Write Drift**: Writing to Postgres and Kafka in the same request without an Outbox table breaks atomicity—if the Kafka publish fails after `COMMIT`, downstream consumers miss the event.

## Tuning WAL, group commit & contention

When transactional throughput hits a wall, profile before relaxing ACID:

- **Batch & Group Commit**: Instead of `COMMIT`ting every single row insert (`10,000` `fsync`s/sec), batch 100–1,000 rows per transaction or rely on `commit_delay` / NVMe storage so one `fsync` persists dozens of concurrent commits.
- **Keep Transactions Short**: Compute hashes, call external APIs, and render payloads *before* `BEGIN` or *after* `COMMIT`. Never hold row locks across network I/O.
- **Transactional Outbox Pattern**: To publish events atomically with DB state changes, insert into an `outbox` table inside the same local ACID transaction and tail it via Debezium CDC or a polling relay.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify `fsync = on` and `full_page_writes = on` (or InnoDB `innodb_doublewrite = ON`) in production configs.
- [ ] Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` (e.g., `30s`) and `lock_timeout` (e.g., `2s`) so stalled callers fail fast instead of piling up locks.
- [ ] Enforce canonical lock ordering whenever a transaction updates multiple rows in the same table.
- [ ] Implement bounded retry logic for `SQLSTATE 40001` and `40P01` at the service boundary.
- [ ] Use `SERIALIZABLE` (or explicit `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` / parent-row locking) anywhere invariants span multiple rows.
- [ ] Keep all external HTTP/gRPC calls strictly outside `BEGIN ... COMMIT` blocks.

interviewProblems.title: ACID Transaction Fundamentals
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on ACID Transaction Fundamentals. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: ACID guarantees that database transactions execute as all-or-nothing units (Atomicity), preserve schema and domain invariants (Consistency), shield concurrent readers/writers from partial state (Isolation), and survive power loss once acknowledged (Durability) via write-ahead logging (WAL), `fsync`, and concurrency control (MVCC/2PL).

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Write-Ahead Log applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Buffer Pool & Heap.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Buffer Pool & Heap experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use `SERIALIZABLE` isolation (SSI detects rw-antidependency cycles) or lock a shared parent row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: ACID is not a binary switch: durability relies on WAL `fsync` before commit acknowledgment, while isolation is a tunable spectrum from `READ COMMITTED` to `SERIALIZABLE` trading lock/abort overhead for anomaly prevention.
Avoid trap: Assuming `REPEATABLE READ` in PostgreSQL is free of anomalies—it is Snapshot Isolation, which still allows write skew.
Avoid trap: Leaving transactions open across external HTTP/gRPC calls, holding row locks and MVCC snapshots for seconds instead of milliseconds.
When to reach for it: Double-entry financial ledgers, wallet transfers, and billing settlements where a debit without its matching credit is catastrophic.
When to reach for it: Finite inventory, seat booking, and quota enforcement where concurrent requests race to claim the last available unit.

putItTogether.title: Putting Acid Transaction Fundamentals Together
putItTogether.summary: ACID is not a binary switch: durability relies on WAL `fsync` before commit acknowledgment, while isolation is a tunable spectrum from `READ COMMITTED` to `SERIALIZABLE` trading lock/abort overhead for anomaly prevention.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Acid Transaction Fundamentals before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Wrapping both `UPDATE` statements in `BEGIN ... COMMIT` with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` (ordered by `account_id` to prevent deadlocks) serializes access to Account A's row; the second transaction sees `$150`, fails the `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint, and rolls back cleanly.
